title: Remove, dismantle and install hydraulic system components of agricultural equipment

lessons.title: The hydraulic system and its dangers
lessons.html:
What the hydraulic system does

Hydraulics use oil under pressure to do heavy work. On a farm, hydraulics lift the three-point linkage, tip a trailer, work a front-end loader, fold a planter and turn the steering. The main parts are:

  • Tank (reservoir) – holds the oil. On many tractors the gearbox is also the oil tank.
  • Filter – keeps the oil clean.
  • Pump – pushes the oil and makes the flow.
  • Control valves – the levers send oil to the right place.
  • Cylinders (rams) – push and pull to lift or move things.
  • Hoses, pipes and quick couplers – carry the oil.
  • Relief valve – protects the system from too much pressure.

Hydraulic dangers

  • Oil injection – a pin-hole leak sprays oil so hard it goes through skin. It may look like a small cut but it is a medical emergency. Get to a doctor at once and say it was hydraulic oil.
  • Never look for a leak with your hand. Use a piece of cardboard or wood, and wear gloves and safety glasses.
  • Falling loads – a loader bucket or lifted implement can drop when a pipe is opened. Lower everything to the ground or block it up with strong stands before you start.
  • Stored pressure – even with the engine off there can be pressure in the system. Release it as the manual shows: switch off, then move the control levers back and forth.
  • Hot oil – let the oil cool before working.

lessons.title: Removing and dismantling hydraulic parts
lessons.html:
Cleanliness is everything

Most hydraulic failures are caused by dirt in the oil. Very small pieces of dirt can scratch a pump or block a valve. So:

  • Clean around every fitting with a brush and degreaser before you open it.
  • Cap or plug every open pipe and port straight away with clean plastic caps.
  • Work on a clean bench, not on the ground.

Removing a part

  1. Lower implements and release pressure.
  2. Put a drip tray under the part. Drain the oil if needed.
  3. Tag each hose and note which port it goes to. Taking a photo helps.
  4. Undo fittings with two spanners – one to hold, one to turn – so you do not twist the pipe.
  5. Support heavy parts like a cylinder or pump before removing the last bolts.

Dismantling

Follow the manual. For a cylinder:

  1. Drain it, clamp it gently in a vice with soft jaws.
  2. Remove the gland nut or circlip and pull out the rod and piston slowly.
  3. Lay out seals and parts in order.

Check for:

  • scratches or rust on the shiny piston rod;
  • a bent rod;
  • scoring inside the barrel;
  • hard, flat or torn seals;
  • cracked hoses, or hoses with worn outer covers or bulges.

Pumps and control valves often need special tools. Ask your supervisor before taking them apart.

lessons.title: Installing, filling and testing
lessons.html:
Installing

  1. Use new seals and O-rings from the correct kit. Wet them with clean hydraulic oil before fitting.
  2. Be careful that seals do not get cut on sharp edges or threads.
  3. Fit the part and start the fittings by hand.
  4. Connect each hose to the right port using your tags. A hose on the wrong port can make a ram move the wrong way.
  5. Tighten fittings firmly but do not over-tighten. Use the torque in the manual where given.
  6. Make sure hoses are not twisted and do not rub on sharp edges or hot parts.

Filling

  • Use only the oil type in the manual. Many tractors use a special transmission-hydraulic oil.
  • Pour through a clean funnel. Keep oil drums closed and clean.
  • Change the filter if the manual says so.

Bleeding and testing

  1. Start the engine at low speed.
  2. Move each ram slowly in and out several times to push out air.
  3. Check the oil level and top up.
  4. Lift and lower the linkage or loader with no load and watch it move smoothly.
  5. Check for leaks with cardboard, not your hand.
  6. Test with a normal load. Watch that the load does not sink slowly when held up.

Store used oil for recycling and record the job on the job card.

Key points

  • Hydraulic oil under pressure can go through skin – it is a medical emergency.
  • Lower or block loads and release pressure before opening the system.
  • Keep everything clean and cap every open port.
  • Tag hoses so they go back to the right ports.
  • Use the correct oil, bleed out air and check for leaks with cardboard.

Use a piece of cardboard or wood

quiz.question: Why do you use two spanners on a hydraulic fitting?

options.text: To tighten it twice as hard
Because one spanner is never enough
To hold one side so the pipe does not twist

quiz.question: What should you do if hydraulic oil has gone into someone's skin?

options.text: Get to a doctor at once and say it was hydraulic oil
Wash it and carry on working
Wait to see if it swells
